14 A car of mass m travels at constant speed up a slope at an angle θ  to the horizontal, as shown in
the diagram. Air resistance and friction provide a resistive force F. The acceleration of free fall
is g.
resistive force F
θ
What is the force needed to propel the car at this constant speed?
A
mg cos θ
B
mg sin θ
C
mg cos θ + F
D
mg sin θ + F

hints: Notice the car moves at constant speed up the slope, so the resultant force parallel to the slope must be zero.
Resolve the weight $mg$ vertically down into components: the part acting down the slope is $mg \sin\theta$ and the part into the slope is $mg \cos\theta$.
Add all forces acting down the slope, the weight component plus the resistive force $F$, to find what the uphill propelling force must balance.
walkthrough: Constant speed means zero acceleration, so by Newton's first law the forces parallel to the slope must balance to give zero resultant force.
Weight $mg$ acts vertically down. Its component parallel to the slope, pulling the car down the slope, is $mg \sin\theta$.
The resistive force $F$ from air resistance and friction also acts down the slope, as shown by the arrow in the diagram.
Total force down the slope is therefore $mg \sin\theta + F$.
The propelling force up the slope must equal this total downhill force for equilibrium: $P = mg \sin\theta + F$. This is option D.

A.explanation: This is the component of weight perpendicular to the slope, which is balanced by the normal contact force, not the propelling force up the slope.

B.explanation: This is only the component of weight $mg$ down the slope, $mg \sin\theta$, and omits the additional resistive force $F$ down the slope.

C.explanation: This adds $F$ but uses $mg \cos\theta$, the perpendicular component, instead of the parallel component down the slope.

D.explanation: The forward force must balance both the $mg \sin\theta$ component of weight and the resistive force $F$ down the slope for zero resultant force.
